title: What can't be measured
hookLine: love, holiness, meaning: science can study their effects, not settle what they are

cards: A chart hangs at the foot of a hospital bed. Pulse. Blood pressure.
Oxygen. Temperature, every few hours, in neat columns. Next to the bed a daughter has been holding her father's hand all night.
The chart is accurate, and it matters; nurses act on it. But it has no row for what's happening in that chair. Near the end of a long run of honest science, a look at the edge of the chart.

teach.b: First, what science does well. It measures. These past weeks have been full of it: heart rhythms, survey answers, death rates, speeches rated by observers.
Science can study what love does, what people who pray report, how a sense of meaning travels with health. That's real knowledge, and worth having.

teach.h: IT CAN'T SETTLE WHAT THEY ARE.
teach.b: Second, what it can't settle. What love is. Whether a place or a moment is holy.
What a life means. These aren't questions of how much; they're questions of what and why. Thinkers differ here.
Some expect science to explain more of this over time. Others hold that questions of meaning and value are a different kind of question altogether, not a gap waiting to be filled.
No side is taken here; the lesson just keeps the two kinds apart. Third, a scientist who lived on both sides. Blaise Pascal was a mathematician who worked carefully with numbers and experiments.

teach.h: PASCAL: THE HEART HAS ITS REASONS.
teach.b: He also wrote, in Trotter's translation of his Pensées: "The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know." He didn't mean feelings beat thinking. He meant some things are known another way.
Fourth, a saying with a lesson in its own history. A popular line, often pinned on Albert Einstein, says not everything that counts can be counted. There's no solid evidence he said it.
So even a saying about the limits of measurement deserves checking. Honest science respects its own edge.

how: Some people who value science and faith keep the two kinds of question apart: they let research tell them what practices do, and look to their traditions, or their own reflection, for what things mean.

games.q: what does “what can't be measured” mean?
o: anything too small for today's instruments to detect
questions like what love is or what a life means
feelings that lab tests show aren't real at all

games.q: what can't be measured: tap the pairs.
p: what and why, not how much
no solid evidence he said it

s: science can study what love does but can't settle what love is
it measures effects. questions of what and why are a different kind of question.
Einstein definitely said that not everything that counts can be counted
it's often pinned on him, but there's no solid evidence he said it.
Pascal meant that feelings beat thinking
he was a mathematician. he meant there are things known another way.

games.q: a friend says, "if science can't measure it, it isn't real." what does this path say?
o: "science studies what things do; what they are is a different kind of question."
games.why: the path keeps both: honest science for what practices do, and room for questions of meaning that a chart can't settle. thinkers differ on where the line is.

practice: Let the numbers of your life drift past for a moment, the bills, the steps, the weight, the hours, and let them go.
Then ask quietly what in your life would never fit on a chart: a person, a promise, a moment you can't explain, something you hold sacred, if you do. Name one silently, and keep it company.

wordCard.voice: What can't be measured. Science can study what love, holiness and meaning do. It can't settle what they are. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: beyond measure. Some of what matters most has no row on the chart. Go gently.
